fun-fact: The Bills are the only team in NFL history to reach four consecutive Super Bowls (1990–1993), though they famously lost all four.
The 1972 Dolphins remain the only team in NFL history to complete a perfect season, going 17-0 en route to winning Super Bowl VII.
The Patriots executed the greatest comeback in Super Bowl history in Super Bowl LI, erasing a 28–3 third-quarter deficit to defeat the Falcons in overtime.
Joe Namath famously guaranteed victory before Super Bowl III in 1969, delivering the Jets their only title and establishing AFL legitimacy ahead of the NFL merger.
During their 2000 championship run, the Ravens set the NFL record for fewest points allowed in a 16-game season (165) and posted four shutouts.
The Bengals famously played in the 1981 AFC Championship—known as the 'Freeze Bowl'—where the wind chill hit -59°F, the coldest game in NFL history.
In their inaugural 1946–1949 AAFC seasons, the Browns went undefeated in championship games, winning four straight titles before joining the NFL in 1950 and immediately winning another.
The Steelers were the first franchise to win six Super Bowls, led by their famous 1970s 'Steel Curtain' defense that featured four Hall of Famers.
In their 2002 franchise debut, the Texans shocked the Dallas Cowboys 19-10, becoming just the second expansion team ever to win their inaugural game.
In 1984, the franchise famously packed up its equipment trucks and secretly moved from Baltimore to Indianapolis under the cover of darkness in the middle of a snowstorm.
In just their second year of existence (1996), the Jaguars upset the heavily favored Denver Broncos in the playoffs, earning the nickname 'Slammers' and reaching the AFC Title game.
The franchise pulled off the 'Music City Miracle' in the 1999 playoffs, using a miraculous lateral on a kickoff return with three seconds left to beat the Bills.
The Broncos hold the unusual distinction of having appeared in eight Super Bowls, winning three, but also suffering three of the top five biggest blowouts in Super Bowl history.
Chiefs founder Lamar Hunt coined the term 'Super Bowl' after watching his daughter play with a popular toy called a 'Super Ball.'
The Raiders were involved in the 'Immaculate Reception' game in 1972, a famous play where Franco Harris caught a bouncing deflection to steal a postseason win with seconds left.
In the 1981 playoffs, the Chargers won the 'Epic in Miami' 41-38 in overtime, a classic where Hall of Fame tight end Kellen Winslow had to be carried off the field due to extreme exhaustion.
The Cowboys recorded an unprecedented 20 consecutive winning seasons from 1966 to 1985, an NFL record that still stands today.
In Super Bowl XLII, the Giants pulled off one of the greatest upsets in sports history by defeating the previously 18-0 Patriots, aided by David Tyree's famous 'Helmet Catch.'
In Super Bowl LII, the Eagles executed the iconic 'Philly Special' trick play, where quarterback Nick Foles caught a touchdown pass on fourth down right before halftime.
In Super Bowl XXII, Doug Williams became the first Black quarterback to start and win a Super Bowl, throwing a record-breaking four touchdown passes in a single quarter.
The iconic 1985 Bears recorded the famous 'Super Bowl Shuffle' rap video mid-season before going on to dominate Super Bowl XX 46-10.
The Lions haven't won a road playoff game since December 1957, holding the longest active road postseason victory drought in the NFL.
The Packers are the only non-profit, publicly owned major professional sports team in the United States, owned by over 500,000 shareholders.
The Vikings have the highest winning percentage and most playoff appearances of any NFL franchise that has never won a Super Bowl.
In 1977, the Falcons defense allowed just 129 points over a 14-game season (9.2 points per game), the lowest points-per-game total allowed in modern NFL history.
In 2015, the Panthers became the first team in NFC South history to win three consecutive division titles, finishing the regular season with a dominant 15-1 record.
To open the second half of Super Bowl XLIV, the Saints executed 'Ambush,' the first successful onside kick attempted outside of the fourth quarter in Super Bowl history.
The Buccaneers began their franchise history with a brutal 26-game losing streak across 1976 and 1977, the longest losing streak in modern NFL history.
Founded in 1898 as the Morgan Athletic Club, the Cardinals are the oldest continuously operating professional football franchise in the United States.
The Rams were the first NFL team to put a logo on their helmets in 1948, after halfback Fred Gehrke hand-painted yellow ram horns onto the team's leather helmets.
The 49ers dominated the 1980s by winning four Super Bowls without losing a single one, propelled by Joe Montana's pristine 11-touchdown, zero-interception Super Bowl record.
In 2011, Seahawks fans cheered so loudly during Marshawn Lynch's iconic 'Beast Quake' touchdown run against the Saints that it registered as a minor earthquake on a nearby seismograph.
The Celtics won eight consecutive NBA championships from 1959 to 1966, the longest consecutive championship streak in North American professional sports history.
In 1976, while playing as the New York Nets in the ABA, Julius Erving led the franchise to a title and won the slam dunk contest by dunking from the free-throw line.
In Game 7 of the 1970 NBA Finals, Willis Reed famously limped onto the court with a severe thigh injury to score the game's first two baskets, inspiring the Knicks to their first franchise title.
Wilt Chamberlain scored an unbelievable 100 points in a single game on March 2, 1962, a record that has never been matched in NBA history.
During their 2019 championship run, Kawhi Leonard hit the first game-winning buzzer-beater in a Game 7 in NBA history, with the ball bouncing four times on the rim before falling in.
Led by Michael Jordan, the Bulls went to six NBA Finals in the 1990s and won all six, never allowing a Finals series to reach a Game 7.
The Cavaliers made history in 2016 by becoming the first team in NBA history to overcome a 3–1 series deficit in the NBA Finals to win the championship.
Known as the 'Bad Boys,' the Pistons swept the Lakers in the 1989 NBA Finals while holding opponents to under 100 points in 13 of their 17 playoff games.
Reggie Miller scored eight points in nine seconds against the rival New York Knicks in Game 1 of the 1995 Eastern Conference Semifinals to pull off an iconic comeback win.
In just their third season of existence (1970–71), Kareem Abdul-Jabbar led the Bucks to an NBA championship, making them the fastest expansion team to win a title in NBA history.
In January 2015, the Hawks became the first team in NBA history to go 17–0 in a single calendar month.
In 1993, rookie Alonzo Mourning hit a 20-foot buzzer-beater in the playoffs to give the young franchise its first-ever playoff series victory over the Boston Celtics.
In 2013, the Heat rattled off a 27-game winning streak, the second-longest single-season winning streak in NBA history.
In the 1995 playoffs, Nick Anderson stole the ball from Michael Jordan in the closing seconds of Game 1, helping the young franchise shock the Bulls and reach their first NBA Finals.
As the Washington Bullets in 1978, the franchise won the NBA title with a 44–38 regular-season record, the lowest winning percentage for a champion in modern NBA history.
In 1994, the Nuggets became the first #8 seed in NBA history to defeat a #1 seed in the playoffs, shocking the Seattle SuperSonics in a five-game series.
Kevin Garnett spent 12 consecutive seasons in Minnesota during his first stint, setting franchise records in points, rebounds, assists, steals, and blocks that still stand today.
In 2017, Russell Westbrook set the NBA record for most triple-doubles in a single season with 42, breaking Oscar Robertson's 55-year-old record.
In 1977, the Blazers won the NBA championship in their very first playoff appearance, led by Finals MVP Bill Walton.
Duo John Stockton and Karl Malone played 18 seasons together, leading to Stockton becoming the NBA's all-time leader in assists and steals, records considered virtually unbreakable.
The 2015–16 Warriors broke the 1995–96 Bulls' record by winning 73 regular-season games, setting the mark for the most wins in a single season in NBA history.
In the 2019 playoffs, the Clippers completed the largest postseason comeback in NBA history, overcoming a 31-point deficit to defeat the Golden State Warriors.
The 1971–72 Lakers set the record for the longest winning streak in North American professional sports history by winning 33 consecutive games.
In 2017, 20-year-old Devin Booker scored 70 points in a single game against the Celtics, becoming the youngest player in NBA history to score 60 or more points.
The franchise holds the record for the longest playoff drought in NBA history, spanning 16 consecutive seasons from 2006 to 2022.
In the 2011 NBA Finals, Dirk Nowitzki led the Mavericks to their first championship by defeating the favored Miami Heat 'Big Three,' posting an iconic fourth-quarter comeback in multiple games.
In 1995, the Rockets became the lowest seed (#6) in NBA history to win the championship, prompting head coach Rudy Tomjanovich to famously declare, 'Never underestimate the heart of a champion!'
In 2021, the Grizzlies set the NBA record for the largest margin of victory in a single game by defeating the Oklahoma City Thunder by 73 points (152–79).
In his 2019 regular-season debut, rookie Zion Williamson scored 17 consecutive points in under three minutes during a explosive fourth-quarter surge.
The Spurs qualified for the NBA playoffs in 22 consecutive seasons from 1998 to 2019, tying the longest postseason streak in NBA history.
Iron Man Cal Ripken Jr. played in an astounding 2,632 consecutive games for the Orioles from 1982 to 1998, breaking Lou Gehrig's long-standing 'unbreakable' streak.
In 2004, the Red Sox became the first team in MLB history to overcome a 3–0 postseason series deficit, rallying against the Yankees before winning their first World Series title in 86 years.
The Yankees have won 27 World Series championships, more than any other franchise in North American professional sports.
The franchise shocked baseball in 2008 by changing its name from the Devil Rays to the Rays and immediately reaching the World Series after a decade of last-place finishes.
In 1993, Joe Carter hit a dramatic walk-off home run in Game 6 of the World Series, making the Blue Jays back-to-back champions on only the second Series-ending home run in MLB history.
In 2005, the White Sox swept the World Series to end an 88-year championship drought, going an incredible 11–1 throughout the entire postseason.
In 2017, Cleveland set the American League record for the longest winning streak in baseball history, winning 22 consecutive games.
In 2012, Tigers slugger Miguel Cabrera won Major League Baseball's first Triple Crown in 45 years by leading the American League in batting average, home runs, and RBIs.
The Royals won the 1985 World Series after rallying from 3–1 series deficits in both the ALCS and the World Series.
The 1987 Twins became the first team in MLB history to win the World Series despite winning fewer than 85 regular-season games.
In 2002, the A's set a then-American League record by winning 20 consecutive games, a streak made famous by their pioneering 'Moneyball' analytical approach.
In 2017, the Astros won their first World Series title in franchise history, powered by an offense that set the MLB postseason record for total home runs.
Two-way superstar Shohei Ohtani made MLB history with the Angels in 2021 by becoming the first player ever selected as an All-Star as both a pitcher and a position player.
The 2001 Mariners won 116 regular-season games, tying the 1906 Chicago Cubs for the most wins in a single season in Major League Baseball history.
In 2023, the Rangers set an all-time MLB postseason record by winning 11 consecutive road games on their way to securing the franchise's first World Series title.
The Braves won an incredible 14 consecutive division titles from 1991 to 2005, a streak unmatched in any major American professional sport.
Despite never winning a division title in franchise history, the Marlins won the World Series twice as a wild-card team, in 1997 and 2003.
The 'Miracle Mets' of 1969 shocked the sports world by winning the World Series after seven consecutive losing seasons since the franchise's inception.
In 2007, the Phillies became the first team in professional sports history to reach 10,000 franchise losses, but capped off the era by winning the World Series the very next year.
In 2019, the Nationals rebounded from a 19–31 start to win the World Series, becoming the first team ever to win all four World Series games on the road.
In 2016, the Cubs ended the longest championship drought in American sports history by winning the World Series for the first time in 108 years.
The 1975–1976 'Big Red Machine' became the only National League team in the modern era to win back-to-back World Series titles with a completely intact starting lineup.
The Brewers are the only franchise in Major League Baseball history to have played in four different divisions across both the American and National Leagues.
In Game 7 of the 1960 World Series, Bill Mazeroski hit the only game-winning, walk-off home run in World Series Game 7 history to defeat the Yankees.
In Game 6 of the 2011 World Series, the Cardinals down to their final strike in both the 9th and 10th innings twice tied the game before David Freese hit a walk-off home run in the 11th.
In 2001, the Diamondbacks became the fastest expansion team in MLB history to win a World Series, capturing the title in just their fourth season of existence.
In 2007, the Rockies executed 'Rocktober,' winning 21 of 22 games down the stretch and in the playoffs to secure their first National League pennant.
In Game 1 of the 1988 World Series, a severely injured Kirk Gibson hit a dramatic, pinch-hit walk-off home run off Dennis Eckersley, creating one of baseball's most iconic moments.
Hall of Famer Tony Gwynn spent his entire 20-year career with the Padres, winning eight batting titles and striking out only 434 times in 10,232 plate appearances.
Barry Bonds broke the single-season home run record with 73 homers in 2001 and went on to set the MLB career record with 762 total home runs.
In the 2022–23 season, the Bruins set the NHL all-time records for most wins (65) and most points (135) in a single regular season.
In the 1974 NHL Draft, the Sabres intentionally drafted a fictitious Japanese player named Taro Tsujimoto in the 11th round to mock the league's slow drafting process.

Red Wings fans established one of hockey's most unusual traditions in 1952 by throwing real octopuses onto the ice, where the eight tentacles originally symbolized the eight playoff wins needed to capture the Stanley Cup.

During their 1995–96 playoff run, fans created the 'Rat Trick' tradition by showering the ice with thousands of plastic rats after player Scott Mellanby killed a live rat in the locker room using his hockey stick.
The Canadiens have won 24 Stanley Cup championships, more than any other franchise in NHL history.
In the 2017 playoffs, the Senators won a dramatic Game 7 in double overtime on a goal by Chris Kunitz, capping off one of the most improbable conference finals runs in modern franchise history.
In 2021, the Lightning became just the second team in the NHL salary cap era to win back-to-back Stanley Cup championships.
Despite having the second-most Stanley Cup titles in NHL history (13), the Maple Leafs hold the longest active championship drought in the league, having last won in 1967.
Following home victories, the Hurricanes popularized the 'Storm Surge,' elaborate and entertaining choreographed victory celebrations performed on the ice for their fans.
In 2019, the Blue Jackets pulled off one of the biggest upsets in NHL playoff history by sweeping the Tampa Bay Lightning—who had tied the all-time regular season win record—in the first round.
Goaltender Martin Brodeur spent 21 seasons with the Devils, establishing NHL all-time records for most career wins (691) and most career shutouts (125).
From 1980 to 1983, the Islanders won four consecutive Stanley Cups and set an unbreakable North American professional sports record by winning 19 consecutive playoff series.
The 1993–94 Rangers ended a famous 54-year championship drought, famously capped off by captain Mark Messier guaranteeing victory in Game 6 of the Conference Finals.
In 1974, the 'Broad Street Bullies' became the first expansion team from the 1967 NHL expansion to win the Stanley Cup.
Mario Lemieux scored five goals five different ways—even-strength, power-play, shorthanded, penalty shot, and empty-netter—in a single game against the Devils on December 31, 1988.
In the 1974–75 inaugural season, the Capitals set an NHL record for futility by winning just eight games and finishing with a 8–67–5 record.
To open the shortened 2012–13 season, the Blackhawks recorded a point in 24 consecutive games (21–0–3), setting the longest season-opening point streak in NHL history.
In 2001, legendary defenseman Ray Bourque finally won his first Stanley Cup in his 22nd and final NHL season, creating one of the most iconic trophy handoffs in sports history.
Brett Hull scored the controversy-laden 'No Goal' in triple overtime of Game 6 in 1999, securing the franchise's first Stanley Cup despite his skate being inside the crease.
The Wild officially retired the jersey number 1 before their first home game in 2000 to honor the team's fans, designated as 'The Team Behind The Team.'
In a tradition adopted from Detroit's octopus toss, Predators fans regularly throw dead catfish onto the ice during home playoff games.
In 2019, the Blues sat in last place in the entire NHL on January 3 before launching an unprecedented comeback run to win their first Stanley Cup later that season.
During their inaugural 2024–25 season, the franchise set a record for the highest attendance for an indoor hockey game in Utah history in their home opener.
During home playoff games, Jets fans unite in the 'Whiteout' tradition, dressing entirely in white clothing to create an overwhelming visual wall in the arena.
Originally founded by The Walt Disney Company in 1993, the team was named after the hit 1992 movie *The Mighty Ducks* before dropping 'Mighty' from their name in 2006.
In 1986, Lanny McDonald scored his final NHL goal in Game 6 of the Stanley Cup Final, capping off his career by captaining the Flames to their first title.
Wayne Gretzky scored an unbelievable 50 goals in just 39 games during the 1981–82 season with the Oilers, setting a record that remains unmatched.
In 2012, the Kings became the first #8 seed in NHL history to win the Stanley Cup, dominating the postseason with a 16–4 record.
In Game 7 of the 2019 first round, the Sharks scored four power-play goals on a single five-minute major penalty to pull off an epic third-period comeback against Vegas.
In their second season (2022–23), the Kraken made history by eliminating the defending champion Colorado Avalanche in their very first playoff series appearance.
The Canucks are the only franchise in NHL history to reach the Stanley Cup Final three times (1982, 1994, 2011) without winning a single title.
In 2023, the Golden Knights won the Stanley Cup in just their sixth year of existence, making them the fastest expansion team in modern NHL history to win a championship.
